chunks: From him, from Abu Ishaq, from Ali ibn Durust, from Abd al-Hamid al-Ta'i, from Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him), who said:

The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whoever brings a debtor to the ruler to make him swear an oath, while knowing that he will swear, and then leaves him (the debtor) out of reverence for God Almighty, God Almighty will not be pleased with him for any status on the Day of Resurrection except the status of Ibrahim, the friend of the Merciful (peace be upon him).'

key_terms.السُّلْطَانُ: The ruler or judge (in judicial context)
key_terms.يَسْتَحْلِفُهُ: To make him swear an oath

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for waiving the right to make a debtor swear an oath out of reverence for God?
ai.summary: In the context of *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith illustrates the virtue of *ihsan* (excellence) in financial dealings, where a creditor voluntarily waives the legal right to compel an oath (*istihlaf*) to demonstrate reverence for Allah. By choosing to trust the debtor rather than enforce a formal oath, the creditor attains a spiritual rank comparable to Ibrahim (AS), the *Khalilullah*, emphasizing that mercy in debt collection is a path to divine proximity.
